content: For confirmatory testing, also referred to as test for triage, detailed information on community-based services and triage testing can be found in the 2015 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services. Close collaboration between community-based testing programs and clinical facilities is essential to ensure that individuals who test reactive in community settings receive confirmed results from appropriate clinical facilities. Additionally, it is critical to ensure that individuals with confirmed HIV-positive results are rapidly and effectively linked to care and treatment services. In generalized HIV epidemics, WHO strongly recommends community-based HIV testing services with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services. This is in addition to routinely offering provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) for all populations, particularly key populations. This recommendation is based on low-quality evidence but is strongly endorsed. In concentrated HIV epidemics, WHO also strongly recommends community-based HIV testing services with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care, alongside PITC for key populations. This recommendation is similarly based on low-quality evidence but is strongly supported. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is a process where an individual collects a specimen, performs a test, and interprets the result independently, often in private. This emerging approach can extend HIV testing services (HTS) to individuals who may be unable or unwilling to attend existing HTS facilities, as well as to those who frequently retest. However, HIVST does not provide a definitive diagnosis. A reactive self-test result always requires additional testing following a validated national diagnostic testing algorithm. Individuals who self-refer for antiretroviral (ARV) drugs after self-testing should be retested according to the national algorithm, starting with the first test. Following further testing, as with all other HIV testing, linkage and referral to prevention, treatment, and care services are advised. Providers distributing HIVST kits should advise individuals with non-reactive self-test results to retest if they have had recent or ongoing HIV risk. Individuals living with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be informed that self-testing may yield false-negative results, particularly when oral fluid-based rapid diagnostic tests are used. Facilityor community-based HTS is preferable for individuals who feel uncertain about or unable to correctly conduct a self-test procedure and interpret the results. Mandatory or coercive HIV testing is never justified. Countries considering the implementation of HIVST should conduct demonstration projects and carefully weigh its potential risks and benefits. More detailed information on HIVST is available in the 2015 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, with updated guidance expected in late 2016. Early HIV testing, prompt return of results, and rapid initiation of treatment are critical for HIV-infected infants, as untreated infants face very high mortality rates in the first year of life. In this population, HIV infection can only be definitively confirmed through virological testing using nucleic acid testing (NAT) technologies. This is because maternal HIV antibodies transmitted across the placenta may persist in the child up to 18 months of age, precluding the use of serological testing for diagnosis. Access to early infant diagnosis (EID) has improved significantly in recent years, but only 50% of HIV-exposed infants were tested by the second month of age in 2014. Delays in obtaining results and further losses in the testing-to-treatment cascade mean that only 30% of perinatally infected infants are effectively linked to services and started on ART in a timely manner. Innovative approaches, such as point-of-care assays and adding a NAT test at or around birth (0–2 days), can improve the rapid identification and treatment initiation in infants. While EID is critical for minimizing early mortality, other testing opportunities are also essential to capture HIV-infected infants and children who are infected postnatally or missed by EID services. In children older than 18 months, serological testing is used in the same manner as in adults, following the nationally validated testing algorithm. Provider-initiated testing is essential to improve the identification of children with HIV, especially those born to mothers who have not received interventions for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). It is strongly recommended that HIV serological assays used for clinical diagnostic testing have a minimum sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 98% under quality-assured laboratory conditions. Similarly, HIV virological assays used for clinical diagnostic testing (usually at or after six weeks of age) should have a sensitivity of at least 95%, ideally more than 98%, and specificity of 98% or more under quality-assured, standardized, and validated laboratory conditions. HIV virological testing is strongly recommended for diagnosing HIV infection in infants and children below 18 months of age. For infants and children undergoing virological testing, assays such as HIV DNA on whole blood or dried blood spots (DBS), HIV RNA on plasma or DBS, and ultrasensitive p24 antigen on plasma or DBS are strongly recommended. All HIV-exposed infants should undergo HIV virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age or at the earliest opportunity thereafter. For infants with an initial positive virological test result, ART should be started without delay, and a second specimen should be collected to confirm the initial positive result. Immediate initiation of ART saves lives and should not be delayed while waiting for confirmatory test results. Test results from virological testing in infants should be returned to the clinic and caregiver as soon as possible, but no later than four weeks after specimen collection. Positive test results should be fast-tracked to the mother–baby pair to enable prompt initiation of ART. Infants with unknown or uncertain HIV exposure seen in health-care facilities at or around birth, the first postnatal visit (usually 4–6 weeks), or other child health visits should have their HIV exposure status ascertained. HIV-exposed infants who are well should undergo HIV serological testing at around nine months of age (or at the time of the last immunization visit). Infants with reactive serological assays at nine months should have a virological test to identify HIV infection and the need for ART. Adding NAT at birth to existing EID testing approaches can be considered to identify HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants. Infants with detectable HIV by NAT at birth are likely infected in utero, progress to disease rapidly, and experience high mortality in the absence of treatment. However, NAT at birth may miss intrapartum infections, and its ability to detect the virus can be affected by maternal or infant ARV drugs taken for postnatal prophylaxis, leading to false-negative results. The ongoing risk of acquiring HIV during breastfeeding can delay the final determination of HIV status beyond 18 months. Identifying the optimal timing and frequency of infant testing remains challenging. Existing testing approaches aim to enhance programmatic simplicity and maximize testing uptake by aligning testing timing with the childhood immunization schedule. Infants with signs or symptoms suggestive of HIV infection should undergo HIV serological testing and, if reactive, virological testing. Children aged 18 months or older with suspected HIV infection or exposure should have HIV serological testing performed according to the standard diagnostic algorithm used in adults. The addition of NAT at birth (0–2 days) can be considered where feasible, but only in parallel with efforts to strengthen and expand existing EID testing approaches. Immediate initiation of ART for infants with an initial positive virological test result remains critical, with a second specimen collected to confirm the result. ART should not be delayed while awaiting confirmatory test results.
